newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Gazprom sees fruits of change soon.
newsitem.headline: Russia Gazprom sees fruits of change soon.

text.p: Steps aimed at turning Russia's huge and unwieldy natural gas monopoly Gazprom into a more efficient, profitable company should bear fruit as early as next year, the company's chairman Rem Vyakhirev said on Thursday.
"By 1998 this company should start to take on a more normal form in line with international standards," he told a news briefing.
An important part of the restructuring plan under development jointly by Gazprom management and the government is to separate non-core business, including construction and agricultural companies.

According to a document studied by the cabinet on Thursday, nearly 50 construction companies not directly linked to the firm's gas output and transport infrastructure will be hived off from Gazprom and turned into commercial entities.
A similar fate awaits practically all agricultural production units, which also became a part of the company as it was formed during the Soviet era.
The company has already created a separate gas trading unit, Mezhregiongaz, which will be made up of around 60 regional arms.
A trading arm of Gazprom has been introduced to reduce debts owed to the company and help it adapt to free market conditions, the document said.
Several major challenges still lay ahead for one of Russia's largest companies, Vyakhirev said.
"One of the basic aims of the restructuring is to reduce gas prices," he said. "We have already started working on this."
Introducing greater competition to Russia's huge gas market was another of the basic tasks of restructuring, said Yevgeny Yasin, Minister without Portfolio and economic guru to the government.
"We (Gazprom, the Fuel and Energy Ministry and the government) will work together on a number of questions, including introducing greater competition. This will be done gradually," he said.
Yasin said restructuring Gazprom and introducing competition into the gas market would not be easy.
"Gazprom is still a strong monopoly. It controls around 95 percent of the gas market in Russia," he said.
Yasin said that as well as lowering gas prices, restructuring would be aimed at strengthening the company's position on the world markets and boosting share values.
He said that Gazprom aimed to cut subsidies to major buyers in order to reduce wholesale gas prices to industrial clients.
